name: Dexatrim

lead: Dexatrim is an over-the-counter diet pill brand sold since the 1970s. People use it to eat less and keep energy up while dieting, to lose weight and body fat.

The original ingredient was phenylpropanolamine (PPA), an appetite-reducing sympathomimetic, removed after regulatory action in 2000. Current versions are blends of caffeine, green tea extract and other botanicals. No trials of current formulations were found, and the individual ingredients have been studied with limited results.

paras: Taken as capsules during a diet, usually timed around meals to curb appetite and lift energy, and combined with calorie control and exercise.

PPA-era use was linked in case reports and a Yale study to hemorrhagic stroke, heart injury and neurological effects. Current stimulant blends carry caffeine-type effects such as insomnia and palpitations, and labels advise caution with heart conditions and pregnancy.

angle.text: Dexatrim is a long-running diet-pill brand used to blunt appetite and add energy while cutting, leading to lower calorie intake and fat loss. Current versions are caffeine and green-tea blends, and no trials of the branded formulas were found.

lead: Dexatrim is a brand of over-the-counter weight-loss products sold as appetite suppressants and energy aids. The line was introduced in the 1970s by Thompson Medical Company and originally relied on phenylpropanolamine (PPA), a sympathomimetic also used in cold remedies [1][2]. After regulatory action in 2000 PPA was removed, and current capsules are multi-ingredient stimulant blends built around caffeine, green tea extract, ginseng and other botanicals [1][2].

PPA-era Dexatrim appears in the medical literature mainly through safety case reports, including a myocardial injury case in a young woman using the product at labelled amounts and a case of transient memory loss and aphasia [3][4]. Researchers also published a pharmacokinetic study of the controlled-release caplet [5]. No randomized trials of current Dexatrim formulations were found, and its individual ingredients have limited evidence for weight loss [2].
infobox: Caffeine, green tea extract, Panax ginseng, DHEA-related ingredients [2]
Chattem acquired Thompson Medical in 1998; sold to NVE Pharmaceuticals in 2014 [2]

paras: Dexatrim is marketed to support appetite control, energy and calorie burning alongside a reduced-calorie diet [1]. Wikipedia lists current capsule products such as Max Complex 7, Max Daytime Appetite Control, Natural Green Tea and Natural Extra Energy [2]. Ingredient lists differ by product, and reported components include caffeine, green tea extract, Asian ginseng and DHEA [2]. Because the products are dietary supplements, the manufacturer states that the FDA has not evaluated its claims [2].

Dexatrim launched in 1976 under Thompson Medical, initially built around PPA [1]. One variant, Dexatrim-18, was advertised as suppressing appetite for 18 hours, and Grokipedia reports that this claim was challenged for lack of supporting pharmacokinetic evidence; Grokipedia is AI-generated and this detail is unverified [1]. In 2000 the FDA asked manufacturers to stop marketing PPA-containing drug products after a Yale study linked PPA to hemorrhagic stroke, and Dexatrim was reformulated [2]. The 2004 US ban on ephedra affected later versions that had used it [2].

A 2003 case report described myocardial injury in a young woman who used Dexatrim (PPA) at recommended doses for weight control, noting earlier links between PPA and hypertension and hemorrhagic stroke, particularly in younger women [3]. A 1984 case report described acute memory loss and nominal aphasia in a 36-year-old woman after using Dexatrim Extra Strength, resolving within 36 hours of stopping [4]. A survey of 100 people with eating-disorder symptoms found that 64% used an herbal product for weight loss, illustrating that such supplements are used in vulnerable groups [6].

For current formulations, Wikipedia lists caffeine-related effects such as insomnia, anxiety and palpitations, and notes possible liver concerns with green tea extract and androgenic effects with higher DHEA intake [2]. Labels advise against use in pregnancy or with heart conditions [1].

No randomized trials of Dexatrim for weight loss were found. Published human work consists of a 1990 pharmacokinetic and cardiovascular-safety study of a PPA controlled-release caplet in 12 volunteers [5] and individual case reports [3][4]. Wikipedia notes that no over-the-counter weight-loss supplement has met criteria for physician recommendation, and that evidence for several of its ingredients is insufficient [2].
